title: My day from morning to night
goal: Describe your daily routine from waking up to going to bed, and master -ся verbs — a family of verbs whose form English has no single match for.
bekal: describe the order of your daily activities
tell apart the pairs учить / учиться and начинать / начинаться
use time connectors: сначала, потом, обычно

dialogs.title: Диалог — An interview for the campus magazine
dialogs.intro: A journalism student, Даша, interviews Ani about her days. Notice the -ся ending on many verbs — and that it doesn't always mean "oneself."

lines.speaker: Даша:
lines.id: Ani, what time do you get up?

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: Usually at seven. I wake up at six, but I don't get up until seven.
lines.literal: usually — at — seven. wake-myself — at — six, but — get-up — at — seven.

lines.speaker: Даша:
lines.id: I get it. What do you do in the morning?

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: I wash up, get dressed, and have breakfast. Then I go to the university.
lines.literal: wash-myself, dress-myself, have-breakfast. then — I-ride — to — university.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: At nine. They finish at three.

lines.speaker: Даша:
lines.id: And in the afternoon? Do you rest?

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: A little. I have lunch, then I study in the library.
lines.literal: a-little. have-lunch, then — study — in — library.

lines.speaker: Даша:
lines.id: How many hours a day do you study Russian?
lines.literal: how-many — hours — in — day — you — learn — Russian?

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: About three hours. Sometimes more, when there's an exam.
lines.literal: hours — three. sometimes — more, when — is — exam.

lines.speaker: Даша:
lines.id: And in the evening? When do you go to bed?
lines.literal: and — in-the-evening? when — you — lay-yourself-down — to-sleep?

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: Late. Around one in the morning. Then I regret it in the morning.
lines.literal: late. around — hour — of-night. then — I-regret — in-the-morning.

notes: **The -ся ending (or -сь after a vowel) originally meant "oneself," but today it covers much more.** ⚠️ English has no single matching form, so learn each of these verbs together with its meaning. The three groups of meaning are in the grammar box.

**Умываюсь literally means "I wash myself."** Compare *Я умываю ребёнка* (I wash the child — no -ся, because someone else is being washed) with *Я умываюсь* (I wash up). This group of meanings is the easiest to grasp.

**Начинаются and заканчиваются are used for THINGS that start by themselves.** *Уроки начинаются в девять* — classes start at nine; nobody starts them, they just start. Compare *Я начинаю работу в девять* — I start work at nine; here someone is doing it, so no -ся. ⚠️ This is often mixed up: if someone **does** it, no -ся; if something **happens by itself**, add -ся.

**Учить vs. учиться — the most commonly confused pair.** *Я учу русский язык* = I'm learning Russian (it has an object). *Я учусь в университете* = I study at the university, I'm a student there (no object; what matters is the place). There's also **заниматься** = to study in the sense of practicing or doing homework: *Я занимаюсь в библиотеке*.

**Часа три means "about three hours."** Flipping the number and the noun turns it into an estimate. *Три часа* = exactly three hours; *часа три* = around three hours. A small trick that makes your Russian sound natural right away. It works with anything: *рублей сто* (about a hundred rubles), *минут десять* (about ten minutes).

**Ложиться спать literally means "to lay oneself down to sleep."** Not just спать. *Я ложусь спать в двенадцать* — I go to bed at twelve. ⚠️ *Я сплю в двенадцать* means "at twelve I'm asleep," not "I go to sleep at twelve."
**Сначала … потом … — two connectors that build a story.** Very useful for telling things in order: *Сначала я завтракаю, потом еду в университет.*

grammars.title: Verbs ending in -ся
body: The **-ся** ending sticks on at the very end, after the usual person ending. After a vowel it becomes **-сь**.
after: ⚠️ **-ться** and **-тся** are both pronounced ***-tsa***, with no separate *t* sound. Russians themselves often misspell them because they sound exactly the same. For you, that's good news: just say *-tsa* and you're right.
**1. Doing something to yourself:** умываться (wash up), одеваться (get dressed), готовиться (get ready).
**2. Things that happen by themselves:** начинаться (start), заканчиваться (end), открываться (open), закрываться (close).
**3. No logical reason — just memorize them:** нравиться (be liked), смеяться (laugh), бояться (be afraid), надеяться (hope), учиться (be a student).

grammars.title: Daily routine verbs
body: The verbs you'll use most to describe your day.
after: ⚠️ Three verbs in the table are irregular and must be learned whole: **вставать → встаю, встаёшь, встаёт**; **ложиться → ложусь, ложишься, ложится**; **спать → сплю, спишь, спит**.
Like English, Russian has its own verb for each meal — завтракать, обедать, ужинать — but it's one word: no "have" needed. A handy shortcut once you're used to it.

sections.title: Telling the story of your day

blocks.text: These connectors turn a list of activities into a story. Use them all in one paragraph and your Russian will instantly sound like someone telling a story, not someone reciting.

blocks.title: A complete sample story — use it as a template
items: *Обычно я встаю в семь часов. Сначала умываюсь и одеваюсь, потом завтракаю. В восемь еду в университет. Уроки начинаются в девять и заканчиваются в три. Днём я обедаю в столовой и занимаюсь в библиотеке. Вечером я готовлю ужин и смотрю сериалы. Ложусь спать поздно, около часа ночи.*

Translation: *Usually I get up at seven. First I wash up and get dressed, then I have breakfast. At eight I go to the university. Classes start at nine and finish at three. In the afternoon I have lunch in the cafeteria and study in the library. In the evening I cook dinner and watch TV shows. I go to bed late, around one in the morning.*
**The most useful exercise in this whole unit:** rewrite that paragraph with your own activities and times. Ten sentences about your own life stick far better than a hundred about someone else's.
